CT4100 Topic Guide

Web search: PageRank and HITS

Use the web’s link graph as evidence of authority and relevance.

Exam-use protocol

Before writing, identify the command word: calculate/trace requires an ordered derivation; explain requires a definition, mechanism and assumption; compare/design requires matched criteria, a justified choice and a limitation. The topic-specific recall and worked routes below are the material to adapt—not text to copy blindly.

Part-by-part recall: definitions, assumptions and mechanics

Definition/equation: PR(p)=(1-d)/N+d sum(PR(in)/outdegree(in)); HITS iteratively reinforces authorities from hubs and hubs from authorities. Links are imperfect endorsements: spam/popularity can mislead. Compare: PageRank is one damped global score; HITS gives two query-subgraph scores. Question cue: translate arrows into updates, iterate and separate link authority from text relevance.

Worked practice 1 — paper-style synthesis (recurring-topic pattern; not a quoted paper prompt) PageRank

Question demand: A,B link only to C; start 1/3; d=.85. Plan/choice: sum incoming shares then damp. Worked answer: PR(C)=.15/3+.85(1/3+1/3)=.617. Mark-winning points: teleport term and outdegree division. Common trap: source sends its full score on every edge.

Worked practice 2 — paper-style synthesis (recurring-topic pattern; not a quoted paper prompt) HITS

Question demand: Explain HITS and contrast PageRank. Plan/choice: define two recurrences and scope first. Worked answer: authorities receive hub links; hubs point to authorities; repeated updates stabilise. PageRank is global/damped/one-score, HITS query-focused/two-score; both need anti-spam and text signals. Mark-winning points: direction correct. Common trap: swap hubs/authorities.

Purpose and module relevance

Web search is an official CT4100 outcome. Link analysis complements text relevance when pages cite or point to one another.

What a question is really asking

Translate a diagram into score updates and explain what links mean. Plan: define nodes/edges; state the iterative update; run one small iteration; compare PageRank with HITS; identify link-spam or topic-drift limits.

Prerequisites, vocabulary and notation

  • PageRank: importance flows through incoming links, divided among a source’s outlinks.
  • Damping: random-jump probability prevents sinks and reflects random surfing.
  • HITS authority: linked to by good hubs; hub: links to good authorities.
  • Both use repeated updates until scores stabilise.

Method: derive a PageRank iteration

  1. Draw directed links and initialise equal scores.
  2. For each page, collect each incoming page’s score divided by its outdegree.
  3. Apply damping: PR(p)=(1−d)/N+d×incoming contribution.
  4. Repeat and compare the change, keeping the total probability near one.
  5. Explain whether link authority should be combined with textual query relevance.

Worked practice 3 — foundational calculation

Question

Pages A and B both link to C only. Start each at 1/3 and use d=0.85. Find C after one iteration.

Model answer

Each incoming contribution is 1/3, so C gets 2/3. PR(C)=0.15/3+0.85×2/3≈0.617. C rises because two pages endorse it; later iterations redistribute scores too.

Question interpretation and independent practice

Build confidence

What is the HITS difference? Check: it has two mutually reinforcing scores, hubs and authorities, usually computed for a query-related subgraph.

Exam bridge

Compare PageRank and HITS for ranking university pages. Outline: graph evidence; one versus two scores; global versus query-focused use; iteration; link manipulation and topical relevance.

High-value traps and corrections

Paper basis for the integrated practice: local 2025/26 PageRank/HITS material was verified; this one-iteration calculation is newly written rather than a paper adaptation.

Integrated paper-style practice - one PageRank update [8 marks]

Scenario. A and B link to C. A has PR .30 and two outgoing links; B has PR .20 and one. With d=.85 and N=3, calculate C's next PR and explain what HITS hubs add.

Question-demand diagnosis: distribute authority over outgoing links, then distinguish hubs from authorities.

Fastest route: add .30/2+.20, multiply by .85, add (1−.85)/3.

Worked answer: C receives .35, so its next score is .05+.85(.35)=.3475. B passes its entire score to C; A splits it. HITS additionally identifies pages pointing to many good authorities as hubs, such as a departmental directory, while the definitive course page can be an authority. Link evidence needs content and spam controls because link farms can distort both signals.

Topic-specific trap: teleportation is not added once for every inbound link.

  • Forgetting to divide a source score by its outdegree.
  • Calling a high PageRank page automatically relevant to every query.
  • Mixing HITS hub and authority definitions.

Final answer checklist

  • Did I state the graph and update rule?
  • Did I show a numerical or directional iteration?
  • Did I explain a limitation?

Past-paper pattern

PageRank and web-search ideas are active in 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26. HITS is lower-confidence, intermittent coverage: revise its contrast but do not rely on it appearing.
